# Findings from the icon study

These are original visual interpretations, not quotations from the book or
claims about the designers' intentions. The study examined a user-supplied
299.97-second recording, retained 70 distinct spreads, and produced 1,306
separately documented printed occurrences. Counts include alternate designs,
repeated sizes, sketches, and tiny comparison-grid examples, not 1,306 unique
apps.

The book is predominantly an iOS reference. Its compositional lessons transfer
to macOS; its historical packaging and effects are not macOS delivery rules.
The private images are not distributed with this skill, and no license to reuse
the pictured artwork is asserted.

Sample keys below use `spread-occurrence`, matching the beginning of each
folder name in the private library. The descriptions make the lessons usable
without that library. Do not infer an app name when only a shape was identified.

## 1. Identity is the part that survives a change of rendering

**Evidence:** Leather and simplified bookmark stars (`004-003`, `004-004`);
stitched and flat rising-bar books (`036-011`, `036-012`); detailed and flat
basketballs (`032-012`, `032-013`).

These pairs keep the bookmark notch and star, the rising-bar rhythm, or the
ball's seam pattern while changing almost everything about the finish.
The successful abstraction is selective: preserve the identifying relationship,
not a random minimum number of paths.

**Transfer:** Write down the invariant before flattening or modernizing an icon.
Compare the old and new silhouettes and negative spaces.

**Failure:** Removing the signature fold or opening along with the texture.

## 2. A shared contour makes a metaphor feel inevitable

**Evidence:** A chef's hat above pepper-shaped moustaches (`047-001`); a rolled
newspaper forming the crossbar of an H (`052-006`); a central fountain nib
between butterfly wings (`070-019`); a contact-card layout toasted into a
sandwich (`070-001`); a whale carrying a grid of containers (`063-030`).

The second meaning lives inside the first object's structure. The image does
not ask the viewer to decode several unrelated badges.

**Transfer:** List the app's actions and physical analogies, then find a contour,
opening, part, or gesture they can genuinely share.

**Failure:** A camera, check, cloud, lightning bolt, and initial all fighting for
the same tile.

## 3. The negative space can be the signature

**Evidence:** The open triangular center of an iridescent loop (`066-012`);
the central keyhole family (`062-009`, `062-017` through `062-020`);
the bear profile (`001-019`); the pale geometric feather (`063-028`).

An interior void or profile often remains identifiable after fine shading
disappears. Its proportions matter as much as those of the solid object.

**Transfer:** Draw the hole or empty shape explicitly. Inspect it at 16 and
32 px and in mono appearance.

**Failure:** A pleasing large cutout closes under antialiasing or tinting.

## 4. Familiar objects need a caricature, not exhaustive machinery

**Evidence:** Cameras dominated by a lens (`027-006`, `028-018`), an oversized
retro radio grille (`054-001`), the piano-key close-up (`055-009`), and a plush
cinema chair with popcorn and remote (`067-008`).

The strongest identifying part gets disproportionate visual weight. Small
controls, seams, and secondary props remain supporting actors.

**Transfer:** Identify the one feature that lets a person name the object.
Enlarge it before adding detail elsewhere.

**Failure:** A technically correct device becomes a muddy cluster at 32 px.

## 5. Material is useful when it explains construction

**Evidence:** A raised circular camera lens (`064-010`), open vault (`039-012`),
metal weight stack with leaf (`059-010`), and draped golden star (`052-002`).

Broad reflections describe curvature; dark joints explain how pieces overlap;
soft folds distinguish cloth from metal. Texture is effective only after those
larger relationships are clear.

**Transfer:** Establish form, camera, light, and material separately. Add
surface detail only where it reinforces those choices.

**Failure:** Uniform gloss, unrelated highlights, or a colored halo pretending
to be contact shadow.

For current layered Apple icons, reserve system effects for Icon Composer.
The historical references demonstrate craft, not permission to double-bake
lighting and shadows.

## 6. Expression comes from proportions, not a large feature count

**Evidence:** Blue robot-bird variants (`015-016` through `015-020`), green owl
variants (`034-002`, `034-009`, `034-011`), smiling headphone device (`056-006`),
and a simple tongue-out green face (`069-023`).

Eye spacing, eye-to-head size, mouth opening, and head contour determine the
reading. A few large expressive features survive where many tiny ones do not.

**Transfer:** Define a facial grammar. Test eyes and mouth on the plain head
before adding material or costume.

**Failure:** A technically detailed face has no clear expression at icon size.

## 7. A family needs invariants and explicit variation

**Evidence:** Robot costumes and rendering approaches across spread `051`;
voxel chicken variants `043-010` through `043-018`; different environments around
the red train in spread `043`; cat emblems in spread `064`.

The variants retain a stable head/body relation, contour, or central emblem.
The surrounding world and finish can change surprisingly far without losing
recognition.

**Transfer:** Specify which dimensions are fixed and which may change.
Compare the family in silhouette before approving themed variants.

**Failure:** Every alternative changes shape, layout, and expression, leaving
only a shared palette.

## 8. A diagonal is a resource

**Evidence:** The large golden paper airplane (`062-005`), red pencil
(`003-015`), pen on coral (`017-006`), carrot (`047-013`), and yellow house-note
crossed by a silver pen (`066-016`).

The diagonal gives long objects room and suggests direction. The tip and tail
need deliberate clearance; supporting objects do not all need the same tilt.

**Transfer:** Balance the diagonal's optical weight and preview the actual
platform mask. Preserve a useful gap around the identifying tip.

**Failure:** The object only fits because its important ends are accidentally
cropped.

## 9. A miniature scene needs one protagonist

**Evidence:** A lighthouse before a full moon (`060-019`), dark pagoda at sunset
(`060-001`), winding mountain roads (`021-009` through `021-020`), and a small
figure in a broad spotlight (`041-029`).

Large depth bands and one high-contrast subject make a tiny world readable.
The scene works because its hierarchy is simple, not because its content is
sparse in an absolute sense.

**Transfer:** Block foreground, protagonist, and background as three masses.
Make the subject legible before decorating the scenery.

**Failure:** A beautiful landscape becomes an undifferentiated patch.

## 10. Color works best as structure

**Evidence:** Colored file stacks (`006-001`), a xylophone (`055-004`), a
segmented spectrum emblem (`049-001`), a fan of leaves (`003-026`, `003-027`),
and the predominantly monochrome robot (`024-009`).

Colors distinguish planes, groups, or movement. The monochrome example shows
that a strong structure does not require a rainbow.

**Transfer:** Choose a dominant field, subject value, and small accent. Give
each extra color a compositional job.

**Failure:** Saturation or a spectrum gradient is the only distinguishing idea.

Do not sample authoritative color tokens from these photographs: warm room
lighting, paper tint, glare, and print reproduction alter the source colors.

## 11. Letters can be objects

**Evidence:** Folded letters (`002-003`, `002-004`), a wooden W (`004-005`),
the newspaper H (`052-006`), and huge numeral pairs (`012-002` through
`012-008`).

The character is a silhouette, construction, or material surface rather than
small interface text. Strong counters and large strokes matter more than
the font's decorative detail.

**Transfer:** Draw or customize a very short mark and convert it to outlines.
Keep the counter open at small size.

**Failure:** An app title is squeezed into a badge and called an icon.

## 12. Repetition needs hierarchy

**Evidence:** Several document stacks (`006-001`, `027-015` through `027-018`),
dashboard panels (`066-003`), and the calendar examples on spread `001`.

One front plane or a small set of large cells establishes the reading.
Rear edges and miniature rules imply information without reproducing it.

**Transfer:** Keep a dominant front layer and consistent offsets. Replace
unreadable data with deliberate coarse rhythm.

**Failure:** Every layer and control has equal contrast and visual weight.

## 13. Scale is a design input, not an export afterthought

**Evidence:** The droplet at several printed sizes (`025-013`, `025-015` through
`025-017`); the dense checkmark grid (`026-100` through `026-183`); the tiny
portfolio grid (`017-100` through `017-135`).

The smallest reproductions support only gross silhouette, color mass, and
contrast judgments. They do not reveal enough detail to justify claims about
texture or exact edge construction.

The checkmark grid also makes a category problem visible: a readable symbol can
still be indistinguishable from dozens of peers.

**Transfer:** Test identity among neighbors and at genuine display sizes.
Use small references to judge hierarchy, not as a source for invented detail.

**Failure:** Enlarging a blurry image is treated as recovered design evidence.

## A practical construction sequence

Concept in words -> three different silhouettes -> value grouping -> optical
proportions -> negative-space tuning -> original rendering -> platform layers
-> actual-size comparison -> one evidence-led revision.

This sequence and the skill's scoring rubric are editorial synthesis. The
examples support the individual observations; they do not prove one universal
recipe or guarantee that every pictured design succeeds.
